query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the degradation behavior of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by the surface’s selective oxidation of the high oxygen‐affinity elements (especially Ti and Cr), which in an oxidizing atmosphere produces a continuous, adherent Cr-Ti-rich oxide scale that restricts further oxygen ingress and limits degradation, while under reducing conditions the absence or instability of such a protective scale leads to enhanced internal (grain-boundary) oxidation and microstructural damage.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured high-entropy alloy with composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 exhibiting a homogeneous, strength‐optimized fcc matrix and minimal pre‐existing oxide coverage.
generation.intervention: Expose identical alloy samples to elevated temperature (approximately 750–900 °C) for extended durations (up to 100 hours) in controlled atmospheres that are either oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen-enriched) or reducing (e.g., hydrogen- or CO-rich environments).
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 750–900 °C, exposure times on the order of 100 hours, and atmospheres differing in oxygen partial pressure to create oxidizing vs. reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or lack) of a continuous, adherent Cr-Ti-rich oxide scale at the surface and along grain boundaries that mediates oxygen diffusion and degradation kinetics.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing atmospheres, the high oxygen affinity of Ti and Cr drives their preferential oxidation at the surface, forming a protective, slow-growing oxide scale that passivates the underlying fcc matrix without compromising bulk strength or fatigue performance. In contrast, reducing atmospheres do not promote stable scale formation, allowing for more rapid oxygen ingress via grain boundaries and internal degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing gases will develop a thin, coherent, protective Cr-Ti oxide layer with limited internal oxidation, preserving the fcc microstructure and mechanical integrity, whereas samples in reducing atmospheres will show more pronounced internal oxidation at grain boundaries and signs of microstructural degradation.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy state with a uniform fcc matrix, minimal pre-existing surface oxides, and high strength/fatigue properties.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should operate under the studied temperature (750–900 °C) and time (up to 100 hours) regimes. Significant deviations in oxide composition or degradation rate outside these conditions may indicate additional processes.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed kinetics of oxide formation, the possible influence of minor elements (e.g., Al), and the specific grain-boundary oxidation pathways remain uncertain. Additionally, quantifying the exact protective effect of the scale under different reducing conditions requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy specimens. Expose one set to an oxidizing atmosphere (air or oxygen-enriched) and a parallel set to a reducing atmosphere (H2-rich or CO-rich) at 800 °C for 100 hours under otherwise identical thermal cycles. After exposure, use surface-sensitive and cross-sectional characterization (SEM with EDS, XRD, and TEM) to analyze oxide scale formation, its continuity, composition, oxide thickness, and signs of internal oxidation. Conduct mechanical testing (e.g., microhardness and tensile testing) to determine any degradation in mechanical properties.
measurements: Chemical composition of the surface and internal oxides
Extent and location (surface vs. grain-boundary) of oxidation
Retention of the fcc matrix phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both oxidizing and reducing exposures yield similar oxide scales and internal oxidation profiles with no significant difference in degradation, or if the oxidizing condition fails to form a coherent protective oxide layer while still preserving mechanical properties relative to the as-manufactured state, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation of Ti and Cr governs protective degradation behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract Oxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr 0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V 2 O 5 , VO 2 , TiO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted.
